samples.brief: Two friends at a railway station discover their tickets are for different destinations.

content.title: Dos billetes, dos destinos
content.story:
Clara y Mateo estaban en la estación de tren. Había mucha gente y apenas se oían los anuncios. Clara llevaba una mochila azul, y Mateo tenía una bolsa con bocadillos para el viaje.

—Nuestro tren sale en veinte minutos —dijo Clara—. Vamos al andén cuatro.

Mateo miró la pantalla de salidas y se quedó quieto.

—¿Al cuatro? El tren a Córdoba sale del andén dos.

—Pero vamos a Sevilla.

Durante unos segundos, ninguno de los dos habló. Después, Clara sacó su billete del bolsillo y Mateo buscó el suyo en el teléfono. Los revisaron juntos: el de Clara decía «Sevilla» y el de Mateo, «Córdoba».

—Creo que nos confundimos —dijo Mateo—. El lunes hablamos de visitar Córdoba.

—Sí, pero luego te mandé un mensaje porque mi hermana nos invitó a Sevilla.

Mateo abrió la conversación. Debajo de la invitación había una respuesta suya: «¡Perfecto!».

—Pensé que hablabas del horario —explicó—. Estaba preparando la cena y no leí todo el mensaje.

Clara suspiró. Tenía muchas ganas de pasar el fin de semana con su hermana, pero tampoco quería viajar sin Mateo.

—Vamos a preguntar si puedes cambiar el billete —propuso.

Se acercaron a la ventanilla. Mientras esperaban, Mateo miraba la hora una y otra vez. Cuando les tocó el turno, mostró su teléfono y explicó el problema.

La empleada revisó los dos billetes.

—En el tren de tu amiga ya no quedan asientos —dijo—. Pero hay otro a Sevilla dentro de una hora. En ese sí pueden viajar juntos.

—¿Podemos cambiar los dos billetes? —preguntó Clara.

—Sí, aunque tendrán que pagar una pequeña diferencia.

Clara miró a Mateo y él asintió.

—Yo la pago. Esta vez voy a revisar bien el destino.

Unos minutos después, salieron de la ventanilla con los nuevos billetes. Mateo parecía aliviado.

—Tenemos tiempo para desayunar —dijo, levantando la bolsa de bocadillos.

Clara se rio y sacó el teléfono para avisar a su hermana de que llegarían más tarde. Antes de llamar, vio un mensaje nuevo: «Cuando lleguen, necesito pedirles un favor».

—Parece que mi hermana ya tiene planes para nosotros —comentó.

Se sentaron cerca de la pantalla de salidas. Esta vez, los dos dejaron sus billetes a la vista.

glossary.meaning: To be in a place or state. Estaban and Estaba are imperfect forms describing background situations.
Railway station.
There was or there is. Había describes the background; hay states what is available now.
A lot of or many; agrees with the noun it describes.
People; grammatically a singular collective noun.
Barely; the announcements were difficult to hear.
To hear. Se oían means the announcements could be heard; the imperfect describes the background.
An announcement, here information broadcast at the station.
To carry or have with you. Llevaba is imperfect, describing what Clara was carrying.
Backpack.
Blue.
To have. Tenía describes a past situation; Tenemos and tiene describe the present.
Bag.
A sandwich, usually made with a bread roll or baguette.
Journey or trip.
Our; Nuestro describes the train, and nosotros means us after a preposition.
Train.
To depart or leave. Sale gives a scheduled departure; salieron is a completed departure in the past.
In twenty minutes; en gives the time remaining until departure.
To say or read as written text. Dijo introduces spoken words; decía describes what a ticket said.
To go. Vamos means we are going, here toward a platform or destination.
Railway platform.
Four, here a platform number.
To look at or check visually. Miró is a completed action; miraba describes repeated checking while waiting.
Departure board or screen showing departing trains.
To become still and remain motionless. Se quedó marks the change; quieto describes Mateo.
Two; used for the platform number and both friends or tickets.
But; introduces a contrast or complication.
For or during; introduces how long the silence lasted.
Some or a few; used here with seconds and minutes.
Second, a unit of time.
Neither of the two. Takes a singular verb here: neither friend spoke.
To speak or talk. Habló is a completed action; hablamos refers to their earlier conversation; hablabas describes what Mateo thought Clara was talking about.
Afterward or later.
To take something out. Sacó is the completed past form.
Train ticket.
Pocket.
To look for or find. Buscó describes Mateo looking for his ticket.
His own one, referring to Mateo's ticket. A possessive pronoun replaces the noun.
Phone.
To check or look over carefully. Revisaron and revisó are completed past actions; revisar is the infinitive.
Together; the masculine plural refers to both friends.
The one belonging to; el replaces billete in references to each friend's ticket.
To think or believe. Creo que introduces Mateo's explanation.
To get mixed up or make a mistake. Nos confundimos means we got confused; here it refers to a completed past mix-up.
Monday. El lunes refers to the Monday when they discussed the trip.
To visit a place.
Yes or an emphatic confirmation. In ese sí contrasts the available train with the full one.
Later or afterward.
To send. Te mandé means I sent you; mandé is first-person preterite.
Message, here a phone message.
Because; introduces the reason Clara sent the message.
Sister.
To invite. Nos invitó means she invited us.
To open. Abrió describes opening the message conversation.
Conversation, here the message thread on a phone.
Below or underneath; locates the reply beneath the invitation.
Invitation.
Reply or response.
His, here describing a reply written by Mateo. Suya agrees with the feminine noun respuesta.
Perfect or great; an enthusiastic expression of agreement.
To think or assume. Pensé means I thought, referring to Mateo's earlier interpretation.
Schedule or departure time.
To explain. Explicó is a completed past action.
To be preparing. Estaba preparando describes an action in progress when Mateo read the message.
Dinner or the evening meal.
To read. Leí is first-person preterite; no leí means I did not read.
All or the whole; todo el mensaje means the entire message.
To sigh. Suspiró is a completed past action.
To feel like doing something or want to do it. Tenía muchas ganas de expresses a strong wish in the past.
To spend the weekend.
With; indicates company or what a bag contains.
Not either; adds another negative idea.
To want. Quería is imperfect, describing Clara's wishes at that moment.
To travel.
Without.
Let's do something; used here to suggest asking for help.
To ask a question. Preguntar is the infinitive; preguntó is a completed past action.
Whether; introduces the question of whether Mateo can change his ticket. Unlike sí, it has no accent.
To be able to or can. Puedes addresses one person; Podemos means can we; pueden addresses both friends here.
To change or exchange, here tickets for a different train.
To suggest or propose. Propuso is the completed past form.
To approach or go closer. Se acercaron means both friends went up to the ticket window.
Ticket or service window where an employee helps customers.
While; connects simultaneous actions.
To wait. Esperaban is imperfect, describing the ongoing wait.
Time on a clock or an hour. Mirar la hora means checking the time; una hora is a duration.
Again and again; repeatedly.
When; introduces the moment something happens. Lleguen after Cuando is subjunctive because the arrival is still in the future.
To be someone's turn. Les tocó el turno means it became the friends' turn to be served.
To show. Mostró describes showing the phone to the employee.
Problem or difficulty.
Female employee, here the worker at the ticket window.
Female friend; the employee is referring to Clara.
No longer or not anymore.
To remain or be left. No quedan asientos means there are no seats left.
Seat.
Another one; here another train, with tren left unstated.
In one hour from now.
That one; refers to the later train.
Although or even though; introduces the condition that makes changing tickets less convenient.
To have to. Tendrán que expresses a future obligation for both friends.
To pay. Pago means I pay, here offering to cover the extra charge.
Small; pequeña agrees with the feminine noun diferencia.
Difference, here the additional amount owed when exchanging tickets.
He; refers to Mateo. The accent distinguishes it from the article el.
To nod in agreement. Asintió is a completed past action.
I; explicitly stated here to emphasize that Mateo will pay.
This time, in contrast with the earlier mistake.
To be going to do something. Voy a revisar states Mateo's intention.
Properly or carefully; describes how Mateo intends to check the destination.
Destination; the place the train ticket is for.
Minute, a unit of time.
New; nuevos agrees with billetes, and nuevo with mensaje.
To seem or look. Parecía describes Mateo's appearance in the past; Parece introduces Clara's present impression.
Relieved; feeling less worried after the ticket problem was solved.
Time available to do something.
For or in order to; introduces a purpose, such as eating breakfast or informing Clara's sister.
To have breakfast.
To lift or raise. Levantando is a gerund showing an action done while speaking.
To laugh. Se rio is the completed past form referring to Clara.
To let someone know that something will happen.
forms: avisar a su hermana de que

glossary.meaning: To arrive. Llegarían means they would arrive, viewed from the past; lleguen is subjunctive after cuando for a future arrival.
Later; here later than originally planned.
Before; followed here by an infinitive.
To call someone by phone.
To see or notice. Vio is a completed past action.
To need. Necesito means I need.
To ask someone for a favor. Pedirles means to ask them; les refers to both friends.
Already; emphasizes that the sister has plans prepared.
Plan or intended activity.
Us; used after para to refer to both friends.
To remark or comment. Comentó introduces Clara's observation.
To sit down. Se sentaron means both friends sat down.
Near or close to.
To leave something where it can be easily seen, rather than putting it away.
forms: dejaron sus billetes a la vista

glossary.meaning: His, her, or their, depending on context. Su refers to one person's possession; sus refers to the friends' tickets.
My; refers to Clara's sister.
Your, addressing one person informally; here Mateo.
And; joins people, things, or actions.
Not; makes a statement negative.

content.title: Dos billetes, dos destinos
content.story:
Clara y Mateo llegaron a la estación con tiempo para comprar un café. Había mucha gente y, junto a la entrada, una familia buscaba sus maletas.

—¿De qué andén sale nuestro tren? —preguntó Clara.

Mateo sacó el billete del bolsillo y lo miró.

—Del cuatro. Sale a las diez y veinte.

Clara comprobó la hora en su teléfono. Después abrió el mensaje que tenía su billete.

—Qué raro. El mío sale a las diez y diez, del andén dos.

Mateo se acercó para leer la pantalla.

—A ver… ¿Por qué pone Valladolid?

—Porque vamos a Valladolid —respondió Clara—. Mi hermana nos espera allí para comer.

Mateo volvió a mirar su billete. Debajo de la palabra «destino» ponía «Salamanca».

Durante unos segundos, ninguno dijo nada. Luego Clara dejó su mochila en el suelo.

—Mateo, ¿compraste el billete para el viaje de hoy?

—Sí, anoche. Pero también estaba mirando trenes para visitar a mi primo en Salamanca. Creo que me confundí al elegir el destino.

Clara miró el reloj de la estación. Faltaban quince minutos para la salida de su tren.

—Tenemos que preguntar si puedes cambiar el billete.

—Lo siento. Tú me mandaste todos los datos y yo no los comprobé.

—Bueno, lo descubrimos aquí y no dentro del tren —dijo Clara, aunque ya estaba un poco nerviosa.

Fueron a la ventanilla de información. Delante de ellos había un hombre que preguntaba por una maleta perdida. Mientras esperaban, Mateo buscó las condiciones de su billete en el teléfono, pero no encontró una respuesta clara.

Cuando llegó su turno, explicó el error y mostró los dos billetes. La empleada comprobó algo en su ordenador.

—Queda un asiento en el tren a Valladolid. Puedes cambiar tu billete, pero tienes que pagar la diferencia. Son doce euros.

Mateo miró a Clara. Ella ya tenía la mochila al hombro.

—¿Lo cambiamos? —preguntó él.

—Sí. Todavía podemos llegar a tiempo.

Mateo sacó su tarjeta y la puso sobre la ventanilla. Clara abrió el mensaje de su hermana para avisarle de que pronto saldrían.

glossary.meaning: Destination; the place you are travelling to.
Railway platform, where passengers board a train.
To get confused or make a mistake. Here, Mateo selected the wrong destination.
To check or verify information.
To change or exchange; here, to exchange a ticket.
A service window or counter where passengers ask for help or buy tickets.
To remain or be left. “Queda un asiento” means there is one seat left.
Used with time to say how long remains before an event: fifteen minutes until departure.
The imperfect describes background or ongoing activity; the preterite presents completed events. Mateo was looking at trains, then made a mistake.

materialIssues: "llegarían" and "Cuando lleguen": future-in-the-past conditional and future-reference subjunctive add grammatical load beyond the guide's emphasis on common past forms. Both are correct and explained, but may require additional support for some B1 readers.
"buscar" — "To look for or find": buscar means to look for, not to find; finding would normally be expressed with encontrar. The contextual explanation of buscó is otherwise correct.
"Pedirles means to ask them": in the sister's direct message, les refers to the two people she is addressing, so the contextual English is 'to ask you both,' not 'to ask them.'

"nuestro" — "and nosotros means us after a preposition": this is correct about nosotros but unnecessarily mixes a separate personal pronoun into the possessive note; nosotros already has its own entry.
"aunque" — "introduces the condition": although is correctly translated, but the additional payment is presented as a concession or drawback, not a grammatical condition.
strengths: Clear misunderstanding, credible explanation, cooperative response and coherent ticket-exchange sequence.
The sister's unspecified favor creates a natural unresolved thread after the immediate problem is solved.
Broad definitions support both common vocabulary and contextual constructions, with generally accurate tense and agreement explanations.
Spanish setting and vocabulary are coherent without assuming Chilean usage.

materialIssues: "el mensaje que tenía su billete": understandable, but an awkward way to describe a message containing a ticket; 'el mensaje con su billete' or 'el mensaje que contenía su billete' would be clearer.
"A ver… ¿Por qué pone Valladolid?": natural Spanish, but the contextual use of poner to mean 'say/read' on a display is unsupported.
"Creo que me confundí al elegir el destino": al followed by an infinitive compresses the temporal relationship into a construction that some B1 readers may need explained.
"para avisarle de que pronto saldrían": the indirect-object pronoun, de que complement and future-in-the-past conditional combine several demands without glossary support.

"Mateo sacó su tarjeta y la puso sobre la ventanilla": the scene stops during the transaction. This is a plausible unresolved action, but offers a weaker continuing thread than a concrete remaining uncertainty or complication.
"glossary": the supplied definitions are accurate, but coverage is too narrow for the learner's explicit request for broad support, including common words.
